doc_summary: A red/blue team auditing game in which blinded auditors tried to detect password-locked sandbagging model organisms among benign decoys with distractor behaviours; black-box methods failed, probes were promising but untrusted, and one-shot on-distribution training worked best. The paper stresses realistic blinded conditions, adversarial red-teaming, and caution about post-hoc success.

items.claim: prefers blinded, adversarial evidence over post-hoc unblinded success because knowing the ground truth makes techniques look better than they would under realistic conditions.
items.quote: Importantly, success in post-hoc analysis with knowledge of which models are sandbagging is not strong evidence that these techniques would have led to a blue team victory under realistic conditions.

items.claim: prefers including benign decoy models with distractor behaviours over only testing positives because otherwise a detector can win just by flagging any oddity or fine-tuning, and false positives go unmeasured.
items.quote: This stress-tests the blue team’s ability to avoid false positives, and prevents the blue team from winning by merely detecting that fine-tuning was performed

items.claim: Distrusts black-box transcript reading and prompt-based elicitation as evidence, since benign models look suspicious and prompting uplifts are not diagnostic.
items.quote: Many prompts elicited comparable or greater performance boosts on benign models, including apparently random, unrelated prompts, which the blue team did not expect to increase the performance of a benign model.

items.claim: Warns that auditor priors shape what looks suspicious: a model that merely differs from expectations gets flagged as misbehaving, so expectation-driven judgments of 'eval-like' or 'bad' behaviour are unreliable.
items.quote: This highlights the role of priors: the blue team were expecting the model organisms to have higher capabilities than the trusted model, and were suspicious when they did not.

items.claim: In a setup, train/construct behaviour by imitating a real weaker model's outputs instead of prompt-distilling instructions to misbehave, because instructed behaviour leaves obviously intentional tells that make it detectable.
items.quote: Unlike Cedar, the prompt-distilled Tarun model of the trial game would sometimes make obviously intentional errors, caused by the explicit instructions to underperform.

items.claim: In a setup, hide triggers/cues in inconspicuous places with no semantic meaning instead of salient visible ones, because visible cues leave tells after training and are visible to auditors.
items.quote: passwords with no semantic meaning at the very start of the model’s inputs were expected to leave fewer cues after training.

items.claim: prefers testing broad and difficult/agentic task distributions over easy benchmarks because errors on hard tasks look more plausible and agentic tasks don't require factually false statements.
items.quote: Mistakes on these tasks were expected to seem more plausible, and it was expected to be more challenging to judge a model’s reasoning steps on them.

items.claim: Treats evidence as convincing only when it is legible, calibrated and validated; unvalidated signals (e.g., probes) are not trusted even when correct.
items.quote: Probes also suffered from issues with legibility, control-distribution calibration, and validation—which in turn made it difficult to trust the results.

items.claim: prefers qualitative failure-mode insights over quantitative claims because a single blue team and ten models cannot support statistical guarantees.
items.quote: The current benefit of auditing games is in surfacing qualitative insights and stress-testing methods in a realistic setting, surfacing failure modes rather than providing quantitative guarantees or a reliable safety case.

items.claim: Gives auditors time limits and realistic affordance tiers (no training, then limited training) to simulate real evaluator constraints rather than unlimited access.
items.quote: These time limits simulate the time-limited conditions of a real testing exercise.

items.claim: Proposes more realistic model organisms that must reason in-context about sandbagging (e.g., via synthetic document fine-tuning) rather than having internalized policies, since direct training may be unrealistic.
items.quote: For future investigations, model organisms could be created using synthetic document fine tuning to investigate whether they can engage in undetectable sandbagging without the aid of a directly internalized policy

items.claim: Flags that proxies (password-locked models lacking self-conceptualisation) may be easier or harder to detect than real targets, so results should be extrapolated cautiously.
items.quote: our password locked models may have been somewhere between benign under-elicited models and coherently scheming models.
